title: Custom system or spreadsheet: which one is right for your business
excerpt: Compare a custom system and a spreadsheet on cost, security, automation and scale, and see which format makes sense for where your business is now.
content:
Choosing between a custom system or a spreadsheet depends on the volume of data, the number of people involved and the risk of mistakes: a spreadsheet works well for small, simple operations, while a custom system pays off when the process grows, involves several users at once or needs access control and automation.

It's a common question in businesses of every size, from shops in Santa Cruz do Rio Pardo to companies that serve all of Brazil. The good news is that the decision gets easier when you compare the two formats on concrete criteria, not on upfront cost alone.

What's the difference between a custom system and a spreadsheet?

The main difference is who controls the rules. In a spreadsheet, control sits with whoever edits it: anyone with access can change formulas, delete data or create parallel versions. In a custom system, the process rules live inside the program itself, with permissions, validations and a change history.

In practice:

  • A spreadsheet is a single file, usually in Excel or Google Sheets, edited by hand by one or more people.
  • A custom system is a program built for your process, with screens, business rules, a database and access defined by role.

It's no surprise that spreadsheets run the day-to-day of Brazilian companies: according to FGVcia's Annual IT Usage Survey, from FGV EAESP, about 90% of end users in the country use Excel to apply analytics to their business. The problem starts when the spreadsheet has to do a system's job.

When is a spreadsheet still the best choice?

A spreadsheet is the right choice when the process is simple, changes often and involves few people. It takes little investment, needs no developer and you can start using it the same day.

It works well in situations like:

  • Tracking monthly expenses for a small business.
  • A task list for a team of 2 or 3 people.
  • One-off quotes and supplier comparisons.
  • Inventory control for a handful of items, checked by hand.

If you're the only one responsible for the data and can check everything at a glance, the spreadsheet does the job. The cost of keeping this format only gets high when the volume or the number of people grows.

When is a custom system worth it?

A custom system is worth it when the operation has outgrown what a spreadsheet can safely control. The most common signs are concrete and easy to spot day to day:

  • Several people need to edit the same data at the same time.
  • Typos or formula errors have already caused losses or rework.
  • You maintain 5, 10 or more spreadsheets that depend on each other.
  • You need history, access control or integration with other systems.
  • The process always repeats the same way and could be automated.

According to the same FGV survey, only 20% of business processes are routine and structured. In other words, much of the work is still handled case by case, and it's exactly when a process becomes routine that it's a candidate to leave the spreadsheet and become a system.

Signs your spreadsheet has become a risk

Some symptoms show you've hit the limit. Watch out when:

  • Nobody knows for sure which version of the file is the official one.
  • Only one person understands the formulas, and the operation stops when they're out.
  • Checking the data takes hours of manual work every week.
  • Information has already been lost through accidental deletion or a formula error.

If you recognized 2 or more of these, the hidden cost of the spreadsheet is probably already higher than the investment in a system.

Comparison: custom system or spreadsheet, criterion by criterion

The comparison gets clearer when you rate both formats on the same criteria:

  • Upfront cost: the spreadsheet wins, since it takes almost no investment. The system has a development cost, spread out over its use.
  • Speed to get started: the spreadsheet, again. A system takes a few weeks to be ready, depending on complexity.
  • Error control: the custom system has the edge, with validations and required fields that block incorrect entries.
  • Simultaneous access: the system, no contest. Shared spreadsheets lead to version conflicts.
  • Automation: in a system, repetitive tasks run on their own. In a spreadsheet, they depend on someone doing them by hand.
  • Security and permissions: a system lets you define who sees and who edits each piece of information; in a spreadsheet, control is fragile.
  • Scalability: a spreadsheet doesn't keep up as the business grows; a system is designed for it.

A note on timelines: the Brazilian government's Governo Digital guidance on hiring systems development services recommends iterations of no more than 4 weeks in projects using agile methods. In practice, this means a well-run custom system project delivers working parts in short cycles, not a sealed package months later.

How much does each option cost?

A spreadsheet costs close to nothing at first, but its cost grows invisibly: hours of manual checking, rework from formula errors and decisions made with outdated data. This cost rarely shows up in any report, but it weighs on results.

The cost of a custom system varies with its complexity, the number of modules and the integrations needed, so it only makes sense with a well-defined scope and a specific quote. What can be said is that the investment usually pays for itself when the system eliminates recurring manual work or cuts losses from errors. That's why the evaluation should consider the return over time, not just the upfront price.

Can you start with a spreadsheet and migrate later?

Yes, and that's usually the most natural sequence. Many processes start in a spreadsheet because it helps you understand your own business: you find out which information matters, which reports you use and where the process gets stuck. After some time in use, that history becomes the brief for the system.

Migration works best when you:

  • Map the current process before building, so you don't automate a mess.
  • Pick a lean first scope, with what hurts most day to day.
  • Plan the move of data from the spreadsheet to the system ahead of time.
  • Have the team test it before you retire the old file.

The most common mistake is trying to copy the spreadsheet into the system, with all the clutter it has piled up. The system should reflect the ideal process, not the workaround.

How do you choose between a custom system or a spreadsheet for your case?

Choose the spreadsheet if the process is simple, individual and temporary. Choose the custom system if the data is strategic, several people depend on it and mistakes are already expensive. Between the two extremes, one question helps you decide: if this spreadsheet were deleted today, how much time and money would your business lose rebuilding the information?

answer_summary: Choosing between a custom system or a spreadsheet depends on the volume of data, the number of users and the risk of mistakes: a spreadsheet works for simple processes and few people, while a custom system pays off when the operation needs automation, access control, history and security. Judge by total cost, not just the upfront price.
key_takeaways: A spreadsheet suits simple processes with few people and individual control.
A custom system pays off when there are several users and a need for automation, history and access control.
About 90% of end users in Brazil use Excel for data analysis, according to an FGV survey, but only 20% of business processes are routine and structured.
Well-run system projects deliver working parts in short cycles; Brazil's Governo Digital recommends iterations of no more than 4 weeks in agile methods.
The cost of a spreadsheet grows invisibly through rework, manual errors and outdated data.
Starting with a spreadsheet and moving to a system later is a natural path, as long as the process is mapped before development.

faq.question: How much does it cost to build a custom system?
faq.answer: The price depends on complexity, the number of modules and the integrations needed, so it can only be set with a detailed scope. The best approach is to ask for a quote after a review of the process. Look at the return over time, not just the upfront investment.

faq.question: Is it worth replacing a spreadsheet with a system?
faq.answer: It is when the spreadsheet is already holding the operation back: several people editing at once, recurring errors, duplicate files and repetitive manual work. If the data is strategic and a mistake is expensive, a system tends to pay off. For simple, individual processes, a spreadsheet still works well.

faq.question: How long does it take to build a custom system?
faq.answer: The timeline depends on the scope, but well-run projects deliver in short cycles. In agile methods, Brazil's Governo Digital recommends iterations of no more than 4 weeks, which means you get working parts throughout development, not everything at once at the end.

faq.question: Can I use a spreadsheet and a system together?
faq.answer: Yes, and in many cases it's the safest transition. The spreadsheet can keep handling one-off analyses while the system takes over the main process, with more reliable data. What matters is deciding which source is the official one to avoid conflicting information.
